Imagine the possibilities. I gotta try this one. Any thoughts???

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Air currents are caused by a differential in air pressure. One way is to have a difference in temperature at different location thus air pressure is changing at different locations. If the entire set up was enclosed so as not to have a differential in temperature or at least slight enough that the air currents are negligible during the exposure time then I think it would work. Thus an insulated enclosure and a mass of steel that would retain the temperature long enough may provide enough stability.

If lighting the object causes a change in mass then why is holography possible at all. Again the exposure time and energy delivered during that time would have to be small enough to be negligible.

Case in point. To the extreem, I believe a Rose frozen with liquid nitrogen with the entire holographic table in a deep freezer would be possible, no? Then the question remains not is the idea "dumm" but to what extent do the variables need to be controlled to make it possible. How cold does the object need to be? What would a differential in temperature of the object and ambient air be considered ok? How long an exposure and at what energy will the set up endure so as not to cause the object to move enough to ruin the hologram? 

I thought about it and as a simple experiement I will take an ice cube, put it on a large steel mass and put them both in the freezer. Then set the plate, let it settle, take the ojbect out of the freezer, place it next to the plate and expose as short as possible to yield a hologram. As a next step re-freeze with a tank around the mass and ice cube to preserve the immediate ambient temperature around the ice cube a little longer. Even if this does not work, I am not convinced the idea is insane or will not work, simply I have not controlled the variables enough.

Should I drill a hole in my freezer?

Should I make an insulated tank?

Not sure, depends when I get bored with this and move on. But it will be fun.

posts.author: alesnick
posts.content_md:
i made a hologram of a frozen ceramic top to a sugar bowl a few years ago

i was doing a series of interferometric exposures -- i _wanted_ the fringes to appear - so i could interpret how various stresses affected objects. I did double exposures of cantilevers with stresses applied and removed, an oscillating tuning fork, and this ceramic bowl. I did an exposure with it thawing, and also another where i heated the object with a lighter in a certain spot

i ended up getting a very bright hologram with a 1.5 second exposure, but with fringes indicating the swelling of the object. Note: i did not freeze the plate or anything else in the setup. the object was not resting on the same surface as the plate either.

the final holograms are on display at my old high school, so i won't be able to take pictures, but i think i have a few pictures of the double exposure cantilevers i could post. the holograms look very similar with respect to the brightness and fringe formation.

alex

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Yes Michael, the ice cube is the kind that comes out of a tray with a rounded bottom. The ice cube is upside down with the rounded bottom at the top in the photo. The separation between the cube and the mount is the horizontal line right at the yellow spot in the center. The mount is cylindrical.

What is really interesting is the part of the hologram where the plate was touching the cold base, that yellow spot. There is actually color there.

There are not fringes in either of the two exposures I made. The first exposure was a settle time of about 15 seconds with exposure of 20 seconds and the second exposure was a settle of 60 seconds with exposure of 40 seconds. This photo is of the second exposure.

I didn't expect it to be that bright as I did not arrange the table for this hologram. I simply tilted my overhead mirror down, set the cube and base on the table, used a support to raise the plate and leaned the plate against the cube/base. This arrangement for the reference beam is for coverage of a 5 x 7 plate and I typically need about 120 second exposure. So thinking about it, I am sure this plate was under exposed. I also did not have enough time to bring my processing chemicals up to the working temperaure I usually use. 

(Edited-Added) Also, the grayish look to the entire hologram with a pretty reflective back is due to the reference beam being almost perpendicular to the plate in the creation. I didn't want to tear down my existing set up on the table.

I put the cube purposely on a steel mount and put both in the freezer such that the mass of the mount kept the ice cube from melting at it's base, thus moving the entire cube. I think an insulator might work but I felt cold mass was best. 

What I was tying to do is take advantage of what I remember about ice. That is, when you take energy (heat) out of water it drops in temperature. Then when it gets to 32 degrees it is still water. Then take a little more energy out and it turnes to ice but is still at 32 degrees. Then more energy out and the temperature falls. What I was hoping, which I think I accomplished, was to allow the ice cube to rise temperature but keep it in the frozen state, thus the massive cold base. Also, this was a perfect time to try this as the temperature in Maryland has been cool, thus the lab was cool and I did not turn on the heat. Ambient temp may have been about 63 F.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
yep, way too ambitious. I'm not going to work out the math, but in a 60 degree F room, an object is going to thaw fairly rapidly depending on the mass. A flower has much less mass than an ice cube or steel plate and will warm much more rapidly. Four minutes may be an eternity in that case.

On the other hand, flowers can (and have) been done by keeping the room as cold as possible and speeding up the processing (in the one case I know of by Lon Moore, by heating the developer).
